0.title: From Eden to the New Jerusalem
0.overview:
The Bible is not a random collection of religious writings. It is sixty-six books written over many centuries by many authors, in different styles and settings. Yet it tells one story. It begins in a garden and ends in a garden city. It opens with God creating the heavens and the earth, and closes with God making all things new. And at its centre stands one person, Jesus Christ.

Many Christians know individual Bible stories well, such as Noah's ark, David and Goliath and Jonah, but cannot see how they fit together. They read the Old Testament as a collection of moral examples, or skip it altogether. Jesus said the Old Testament was about him: it is they that bear witness about me (John 5:39). After his resurrection, beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, he interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself (Luke 24:27).

This study traces the great storyline from beginning to end. Knowing it helps us read any passage in its place, see how the promises build, and understand why Christ is the climax of everything.

Six units: (1) Creation and Fall; (2) The Promise to Abraham; (3) A People, a Law and a Land; (4) Kings, Prophets and Exile; (5) The Promise Kept in Christ; (6) To the Nations and the New Creation.

1.title: Creation and Fall
1.overview:
God's good world. The story begins with God creating everything good. He made humanity in his image and placed them in a garden, where they lived in his presence, under his word and with a task to fill and rule the earth. This is the world as it was meant to be: God's people, in God's place, under God's rule, enjoying his blessing.

The fall. Adam and Eve rejected God's word and ate the forbidden fruit. They were driven from God's presence, out of the garden. Death entered the world. Their son Cain murdered his brother. By the time of Noah, the earth was filled with violence, and God judged it with the flood (Gen 6-9).

The promise. Yet in the very moment of judgment, God promised that the offspring of the woman would crush the serpent's head (Gen 3:15). The rest of the Bible traces how God keeps that promise.

Babel. After the flood, humanity united to build a tower to make a name for themselves (Gen 11:4). God scattered them and confused their languages. Humanity was divided and far from God. The question hanging over Genesis 1-11 is: how will God bless a cursed world?

The opening chapters set up the whole story. The rest of Scripture is about God bringing a people back into his presence, under his rule, in a renewed world. Everything that was lost in Eden will be restored, and more.
1.theology:
Kingdom pattern: One helpful way to see the story is through the kingdom of God: God's people, in God's place, under God's rule and blessing. Eden had all four. The fall lost them. The rest of the Bible shows God restoring them, finally and fully in the new creation.

Judgment and grace: From the beginning, the story combines judgment and grace. God judges sin, but he never abandons his purpose. Every judgment in Genesis 1-11 is followed by an act of mercy: clothing for Adam and Eve, protection for Cain, rescue for Noah.

The first gospel: The Creation and the Fall study covers Genesis 1-3 in more depth.
1.examples:
Then: After the flood, God made a covenant with Noah and every living creature, promising never again to destroy the earth with a flood. He set his bow in the clouds as a sign (Gen 9:12-17). Even in a fallen world, God commits himself to preserve creation so that his plan of salvation can unfold.

Now: A new Christian has been reading the Bible from the beginning and is confused by Genesis 1-11. A friend explains that these chapters set the stage: a good creation, a terrible fall and a promise of rescue. Suddenly the rest of the Bible starts to make sense.

A simple test: Can you summarise the first eleven chapters of Genesis in three sentences?

verseByVerse.quote: Then God said, "Let us make man in our image, after our likeness. And let them have dominion over the fish of the sea and over the birds of the heavens and over the livestock and over all the earth and over every creeping thing that creeps on the earth." So God created man in his own image, in the image of God he created him; male and female he created them. And God blessed them. And God said to them, "Be fruitful and multiply and fill the earth and subdue it, and have dominion over the fish of the sea and over the birds of the heavens and over every living thing that moves on the earth." And God said, "Behold, I have given you every plant yielding seed that is on the face of all the earth, and every tree with seed in its fruit. You shall have them for food. And to every beast of the earth and to every bird of the heavens and to everything that creeps on the earth, everything that has the breath of life, I have given every green plant for food." And it was so. And God saw everything that he had made, and behold, it was very good. And there was evening and there was morning, the sixth day. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The story begins at its high point. Humanity is made in God's image, blessed and given dominion. God provides food for every creature. Everything is very good. This is the world God made, and it is the world he will restore.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD God said to the serpent, "Because you have done this, cursed are you above all livestock and above all beasts of the field; on your belly you shall go, and dust you shall eat all the days of your life. I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your offspring and her offspring; he shall bruise your head, and you shall bruise his heel." To the woman he said, "I will surely multiply your pain in childbearing; in pain you shall bring forth children. Your desire shall be for your husband, and he shall rule over you." And to Adam he said, "Because you have listened to the voice of your wife and have eaten of the tree of which I commanded you, 'You shall not eat of it,' cursed is the ground because of you; in pain you shall eat of it all the days of your life; thorns and thistles it shall bring forth for you; and you shall eat the plants of the field. By the sweat of your face you shall eat bread, till you return to the ground, for out of it you were taken; for you are dust, and to dust you shall return." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The consequences of the fall fall on the serpent, the woman, the man and the ground. But in the curse on the serpent there is a promise: the woman's offspring will crush its head. From this point on, the Bible is watching for that offspring.

verseByVerse.quote: Then God said to Noah and to his sons with him, "Behold, I establish my covenant with you and your offspring after you, and with every living creature that is with you, the birds, the livestock, and every beast of the earth with you, as many as came out of the ark; it is for every beast of the earth. I establish my covenant with you, that never again shall all flesh be cut off by the waters of the flood, and never again shall there be a flood to destroy the earth." And God said, "This is the sign of the covenant that I make between me and you and every living creature that is with you, for all future generations: I have set my bow in the cloud, and it shall be a sign of the covenant between me and the earth. When I bring clouds over the earth and the bow is seen in the clouds, I will remember my covenant that is between me and you and every living creature of all flesh. And the waters shall never again become a flood to destroy all flesh. When the bow is in the clouds, I will see it and remember the everlasting covenant between God and every living creature of all flesh that is on the earth." God said to Noah, "This is the sign of the covenant that I have established between me and all flesh that is on the earth." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: God's covenant with Noah is made with all creation. He promises never again to flood the earth, and sets the rainbow as a sign. This covenant of preservation keeps the world stable so that God's promises of salvation can be fulfilled.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the whole earth had one language and the same words. And as people migrated from the east, they found a plain in the land of Shinar and settled there. And they said to one another, "Come, let us make bricks, and burn them thoroughly." And they had brick for stone, and bitumen for mortar. Then they said, "Come, let us build ourselves a city and a tower with its top in the heavens, and let us make a name for ourselves, lest we be dispersed over the face of the whole earth." And the LORD came down to see the city and the tower, which the children of man had built. And the LORD said, "Behold, they are one people, and they have all one language, and this is only the beginning of what they will do. And nothing that they propose to do will now be impossible for them. Come, let us go down and there confuse their language, so that they may not understand one another's speech." So the LORD dispersed them from there over the face of all the earth, and they left off building the city. Therefore its name was called Babel, because there the LORD confused the language of all the earth. And from there the LORD dispersed them over the face of all the earth. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Humanity unites to build a tower and make a name for itself. God comes down, confuses their languages and scatters them. Pride brings division. This scattering will be reversed at Pentecost, when the gospel is heard in many languages (Acts 2).

1.reflection:
What was lost in the fall? List as many things as you can.

How does Genesis 3:15 set up the rest of the Bible?

What patterns of judgment and grace do you see in Genesis 1-11?

How does Babel connect to Pentecost?

2.title: The Promise to Abraham
2.overview:
In Genesis 12, the story narrows to one man. God called Abram from Ur and made him a great promise: Now the LORD said to Abram, "Go from your country and your kindred and your father's house to the land that I will show you. And I will make of you a great nation, and I will bless you and make your name great, so that you will be a blessing. I will bless those who bless you, and him who dishonors you I will curse, and in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed." (Gen 12:1-3).

Three promises. God promised Abraham a people (a great nation, descendants as many as the stars), a land (Canaan) and blessing, including blessing for all the families of the earth through him. Where Babel tried to make a name for itself, God would make Abraham's name great. Where Babel scattered, God would bless all nations.

Faith. Abraham was old and childless. Yet when God promised him descendants as numerous as the stars, he believed the LORD, and he counted it to him as righteousness (Gen 15:6). Paul later uses this verse as the foundation of justification by faith (Rom 4:3).

Covenant. God bound himself to Abraham in covenant. In a strange ceremony, God alone passed between the pieces of the sacrificed animals (Gen 15:17), taking the whole obligation on himself.

The promised son. After twenty-five years of waiting, Isaac was born. Then God tested Abraham, telling him to offer Isaac as a sacrifice. At the last moment God provided a ram instead. Abraham called the place The LORD will provide (Gen 22:14). Two thousand years later, on a hill in the same region, God did not spare his own Son.

The promise passed on. The promises passed from Abraham to Isaac, to Jacob (renamed Israel) and to his twelve sons. Genesis ends with Jacob's family in Egypt, a small clan waiting for God to fulfil his word.
2.theology:
The gospel preached beforehand: Paul says Scripture preached the gospel beforehand to Abraham, saying, "In you shall all the nations be blessed." (Gal 3:8). The promise to bless the nations is fulfilled when Gentiles believe in Christ.

The true offspring: Paul notes that the promise was made to Abraham's offspring, singular, who is Christ (Gal 3:16). And all who belong to Christ are Abraham's offspring, heirs according to the promise (Gal 3:29).

Typology: Many Old Testament people and events point forward to Christ, not by allegory, but because God shapes history in patterns. Isaac carrying the wood up the mountain, and the ram provided in his place, foreshadow the cross.
2.examples:
Then: Abraham's grandson Jacob was a deceiver, yet God chose him and renewed the promise to him at Bethel (Gen 28:13-15). God's promises do not depend on the worthiness of those who receive them.

Now: A Gentile believer reads Galatians 3 and realises that he is a son of Abraham through faith in Christ. The promise God made to an old man in the Middle East thousands of years ago includes him. He feels part of a story far bigger than himself.

A simple test: How is the promise to Abraham fulfilled in your life as a Christian?

verseByVerse.quote: Now the LORD said to Abram, "Go from your country and your kindred and your father's house to the land that I will show you. And I will make of you a great nation, and I will bless you and make your name great, so that you will be a blessing. I will bless those who bless you, and him who dishonors you I will curse, and in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: God's call to Abram is the turning point of Genesis. After the curses of Genesis 3-11, the word "bless" appears five times in these three verses. God will bless Abram, make him a blessing and bless all families of the earth through him. The answer to Babel is grace.

verseByVerse.quote: After these things the word of the LORD came to Abram in a vision: "Fear not, Abram, I am your shield; your reward shall be very great." But Abram said, "O Lord GOD, what will you give me, for I continue childless, and the heir of my house is Eliezer of Damascus?" And Abram said, "Behold, you have given me no offspring, and a member of my household will be my heir." And behold, the word of the LORD came to him: "This man shall not be your heir; your very own son shall be your heir." And he brought him outside and said, "Look toward heaven, and number the stars, if you are able to number them." Then he said to him, "So shall your offspring be." And he believed the LORD, and he counted it to him as righteousness. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Abram, still childless, questions God. God takes him outside and tells him to count the stars: so shall your offspring be. Abram believed, and God counted it to him as righteousness. Faith in God's promise has always been the way of salvation.

verseByVerse.quote: When they came to the place of which God had told him, Abraham built the altar there and laid the wood in order and bound Isaac his son and laid him on the altar, on top of the wood. Then Abraham reached out his hand and took the knife to slaughter his son. But the angel of the LORD called to him from heaven and said, "Abraham, Abraham!" And he said, "Here I am." He said, "Do not lay your hand on the boy or do anything to him, for now I know that you fear God, seeing you have not withheld your son, your only son, from me." And Abraham lifted up his eyes and looked, and behold, behind him was a ram, caught in a thicket by his horns. And Abraham went and took the ram and offered it up as a burnt offering instead of his son. So Abraham called the name of that place, "The LORD will provide"; as it is said to this day, "On the mount of the LORD it shall be provided." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Abraham obeyed the hardest command imaginable. As he raised the knife, the angel of the LORD stopped him. A ram caught in a thicket took Isaac's place. Abraham named the place for God's provision. This story points to the cross, where God provided his own Son as the substitute.

verseByVerse.quote: Know then that it is those of faith who are the sons of Abraham. And the Scripture, foreseeing that God would justify the Gentiles by faith, preached the gospel beforehand to Abraham, saying, "In you shall all the nations be blessed." So then, those who are of faith are blessed along with Abraham, the man of faith. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul explains that those of faith are the true sons of Abraham. Scripture foresaw that God would justify the Gentiles by faith, and preached the gospel to Abraham in advance. Those who believe are blessed with Abraham. The promise of Genesis 12 reaches all believers.

2.reflection:
What three promises did God make to Abraham?

Why does Paul call Genesis 12:3 the gospel preached beforehand?

How does Genesis 22 point to Christ?

What does it mean for you to be a child of Abraham by faith?

3.title: A People, a Law and a Land
3.overview:
Slavery and rescue. Abraham's descendants multiplied in Egypt, but a new Pharaoh enslaved them. God heard their cry and remembered his covenant with Abraham (Exod 2:24). He raised up Moses and sent plagues on Egypt. On the night of the Passover, the blood of a lamb on the doorposts protected Israel's firstborn from judgment. God led his people through the Red Sea and destroyed Pharaoh's army. The exodus became the great picture of salvation for the rest of the Bible.

Covenant at Sinai. At Mount Sinai, God made a covenant with Israel. He reminded them of his grace: You yourselves have seen what I did to the Egyptians, and how I bore you on eagles' wings and brought you to myself (Exod 19:4). He called them to be a kingdom of priests and a holy nation (Exod 19:6). And he gave them his law, including the Ten Commandments, to shape them as his people.

God in their midst. God commanded the building of the tabernacle, a portable tent where he would dwell among his people. At its heart was the Most Holy Place, where his presence rested. The sacrificial system taught that sinners can only approach a holy God through the shedding of blood. Something of Eden's closeness to God was being restored, though behind a curtain.

The wilderness. Israel repeatedly grumbled and rebelled. Because they refused to trust God and enter the land, that generation died in the wilderness over forty years (Num 14).

The land. Under Joshua, the next generation entered Canaan. God gave them the land he had promised to Abraham. Not one word of all the good promises that the LORD had made to the house of Israel had failed; all came to pass (Josh 21:45). God's people were now in God's place, under his rule.
3.theology:
The exodus pattern: The exodus shapes later hope. The prophets promised a new exodus from exile. At the transfiguration, Moses and Elijah spoke with Jesus about his departure (Luke 9:31); he was crucified at Passover, and is called our Passover lamb (1 Cor 5:7). Salvation in Christ is the greater exodus from slavery to sin.

Law and grace: The law was given after the rescue, not as the way to earn it. It showed Israel how to live as God's redeemed people. It also revealed sin and pointed to the need for a better sacrifice and a better heart (Heb 10:1-4).

Tabernacle to temple to Christ: God's dwelling with his people moves from tabernacle, to temple, to Christ who dwelt among us (John 1:14), to the church as God's temple, and finally to the new creation, where the whole city is the dwelling of God (Rev 21:3).
3.examples:
Then: On the night of the first Passover, every Israelite family killed a lamb and put its blood on their doorposts. God said, when I see the blood, I will pass over you (Exod 12:13). Centuries later John the Baptist pointed to Jesus: Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world! (John 1:29).

Now: A believer reads Exodus for the first time and sees the gospel everywhere: slavery, a lamb, blood, rescue, a law of love, God dwelling with his people. Her Lord's Supper next Sunday takes on new meaning as she remembers Christ, our Passover.

A simple test: In what ways is your salvation like the exodus?

verseByVerse.quote: Then Moses called all the elders of Israel and said to them, "Go and select lambs for yourselves according to your clans, and kill the Passover lamb. Take a bunch of hyssop and dip it in the blood that is in the basin, and touch the lintel and the two doorposts with the blood that is in the basin. None of you shall go out of the door of his house until the morning. For the LORD will pass through to strike the Egyptians, and when he sees the blood on the lintel and on the two doorposts, the LORD will pass over the door and will not allow the destroyer to enter your houses to strike you. You shall observe this rite as a statute for you and for your sons forever. And when you come to the land that the LORD will give you, as he has promised, you shall keep this service. And when your children say to you, 'What do you mean by this service?' you shall say, 'It is the sacrifice of the LORD's Passover, for he passed over the houses of the people of Israel in Egypt, when he struck the Egyptians but spared our houses.'" And the people bowed their heads and worshiped. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Moses instructs the elders to kill the Passover lamb and put its blood on the doorposts. The LORD will pass over the doors marked by blood. Israel is to keep this feast forever and explain it to their children. The Passover anticipates the death of Christ, the true lamb.

verseByVerse.quote: while Moses went up to God. The LORD called to him out of the mountain, saying, "Thus you shall say to the house of Jacob, and tell the people of Israel: 'You yourselves have seen what I did to the Egyptians, and how I bore you on eagles' wings and brought you to myself. Now therefore, if you will indeed obey my voice and keep my covenant, you shall be my treasured possession among all peoples, for all the earth is mine; and you shall be to me a kingdom of priests and a holy nation.' These are the words that you shall speak to the people of Israel." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: God reminds Israel of the rescue from Egypt and how he carried them to himself. Then he calls them to obey his covenant and be his treasured possession, a kingdom of priests and a holy nation. Peter later applies these titles to the church (1 Pet 2:9).

verseByVerse.quote: Then the cloud covered the tent of meeting, and the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle. And Moses was not able to enter the tent of meeting because the cloud settled on it, and the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle. Throughout all their journeys, whenever the cloud was taken up from over the tabernacle, the people of Israel would set out. But if the cloud was not taken up, then they did not set out till the day that it was taken up. For the cloud of the LORD was on the tabernacle by day, and fire was in it by night, in the sight of all the house of Israel throughout all their journeys. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: When the tabernacle was finished, the cloud covered it and the glory of the LORD filled it. God's presence dwelt among his people, leading them on their journey. This is a partial restoration of Eden's fellowship with God.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus the LORD gave to Israel all the land that he swore to give to their fathers. And they took possession of it, and they settled there. And the LORD gave them rest on every side just as he had sworn to their fathers. Not one of all their enemies had withstood them, for the LORD had given all their enemies into their hands. Not one word of all the good promises that the LORD had made to the house of Israel had failed; all came to pass. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The LORD gave Israel all the land he had sworn to their fathers. He gave them rest and defeated their enemies. Not one of his good promises failed. God's faithfulness to Abraham was proven in history.

3.reflection:
How does the exodus picture salvation in Christ?

Why was the law given after the rescue from Egypt, not before?

Trace God's dwelling with his people from Eden to the new creation.

How does Joshua 21:45 encourage you to trust God's promises?

4.title: Kings, Prophets and Exile
4.overview:
Judges. After Joshua, Israel fell into a cycle of sin, oppression, crying out and rescue. In those days there was no king in Israel. Everyone did what was right in his own eyes (Judg 21:25). The book of Judges shows that Israel needed a righteous king.

The kingdom. Israel demanded a king like the nations. Saul began well but disobeyed God. Then God chose David, a shepherd boy, a man after his own heart (1 Sam 13:14). Under David and his son Solomon, the kingdom reached its height. Solomon built the temple, and God's glory filled it.

The promise to David. God made a covenant with David: And your house and your kingdom shall be made sure forever before me. Your throne shall be established forever (2 Sam 7:16). A son of David would reign forever. From then on, Israel's hope focused on a coming king from David's line, the Messiah.

Division and decline. Solomon turned to idols late in life, and after his death the kingdom split in two: Israel in the north and Judah in the south. Most kings led the people into idolatry. God sent prophets such as Elijah, Isaiah, Jeremiah and many others to call them back, warning of judgment and promising future restoration.

Exile. The northern kingdom fell to Assyria. Later Judah fell to Babylon. Jerusalem and the temple were destroyed, and the people were carried into exile. It seemed that God's promises had failed. God's people were out of God's place, and the line of David seemed cut off.

Promises of a new day. Yet in the darkness, the prophets promised a new exodus, a new covenant, a new heart, a suffering servant who would bear sins, a son of David who would reign in justice and the Spirit poured out on all flesh. Some exiles returned to rebuild Jerusalem, but the Old Testament ends still waiting.
4.theology:
The failure of the old covenant: Israel's history shows that the problem is the human heart. Even with the law, the temple and kings, the people turned away. This pointed to the need for a new covenant, in which God would write his law on hearts (Jer 31:33) and give his Spirit (Ezek 36:27).

Prophet, priest and king: Israel's three great offices all failed in various ways. They pointed to the one who would fulfil all three perfectly: Jesus Christ.

The waiting: The four hundred years between the Old and New Testaments are often called the silent years. The people waited for the Messiah, the coming of the kingdom and the end of exile.
4.examples:
Then: Daniel in exile in Babylon read Jeremiah's prophecy that the exile would last seventy years. He confessed the sins of his people and prayed for God to act (Dan 9). He lived faithfully in a foreign land, waiting for God's promises.

Now: A Christian reads 1 and 2 Kings and finds it depressing: king after king doing evil. Then she reads Isaiah 9:6-7 and realises that the failure of these kings was preparing the way for the perfect King. Her reading of the Old Testament changes from moral lessons to waiting for Christ.

A simple test: How do the failures of Israel's kings make you long for Christ?

verseByVerse.quote: When your days are fulfilled and you lie down with your fathers, I will raise up your offspring after you, who shall come from your body, and I will establish his kingdom. He shall build a house for my name, and I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever. I will be to him a father, and he shall be to me a son. When he commits iniquity, I will discipline him with the rod of men, with the stripes of the sons of men, but my steadfast love will not depart from him, as I took it from Saul, whom I put away from before you. And your house and your kingdom shall be made sure forever before me. Your throne shall be established forever.'" (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: God promises David an offspring whose kingdom will be established forever. God will be his Father, and he will be God's son. David's throne will endure forever. This promise shaped all of Israel's later hope and is fulfilled in Jesus, the Son of David and Son of God.

verseByVerse.quote: For to us a child is born, to us a son is given; and the government shall be upon his shoulder, and his name shall be called Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace. Of the increase of his government and of peace there will be no end, on the throne of David and over his kingdom, to establish it and to uphold it with justice and with righteousness from this time forth and forevermore. The zeal of the LORD of hosts will do this. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: In a dark time, Isaiah announces a child born, a son given, with names that belong to God: Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace. He will sit on David's throne and reign forever with justice. This is the hope the exile could not destroy.

verseByVerse.quote: "Behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel and the house of Judah, not like the covenant that I made with their fathers on the day when I took them by the hand to bring them out of the land of Egypt, my covenant that they broke, though I was their husband, declares the LORD. For this is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days, declares the LORD: I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts. And I will be their God, and they shall be my people. And no longer shall each one teach his neighbor and each his brother, saying, 'Know the LORD,' for they shall all know me, from the least of them to the greatest, declares the LORD. For I will forgive their iniquity, and I will remember their sin no more." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: God promises a new covenant, unlike the one Israel broke at Sinai. He will write his law on their hearts, all will know him, and he will remember their sins no more. Jesus announced this new covenant at the Last Supper (Luke 22:20).

verseByVerse.quote: The hand of the LORD was upon me, and he brought me out in the Spirit of the LORD and set me down in the middle of the valley; it was full of bones. And he led me around among them, and behold, there were very many on the surface of the valley, and behold, they were very dry. And he said to me, "Son of man, can these bones live?" And I answered, "O Lord GOD, you know." Then he said to me, "Prophesy over these bones, and say to them, O dry bones, hear the word of the LORD. Thus says the Lord GOD to these bones: Behold, I will cause breath to enter you, and you shall live. And I will lay sinews upon you, and will cause flesh to come upon you, and cover you with skin, and put breath in you, and you shall live, and you shall know that I am the LORD." So I prophesied as I was commanded. And as I prophesied, there was a sound, and behold, a rattling, and the bones came together, bone to its bone. And I looked, and behold, there were sinews on them, and flesh had come upon them, and skin had covered them. But there was no breath in them. Then he said to me, "Prophesy to the breath; prophesy, son of man, and say to the breath, Thus says the Lord GOD: Come from the four winds, O breath, and breathe on these slain, that they may live." So I prophesied as he commanded me, and the breath came into them, and they lived and stood on their feet, an exceedingly great army. Then he said to me, "Son of man, these bones are the whole house of Israel. Behold, they say, 'Our bones are dried up, and our hope is lost; we are indeed cut off.' Therefore prophesy, and say to them, Thus says the Lord GOD: Behold, I will open your graves and raise you from your graves, O my people. And I will bring you into the land of Israel. And you shall know that I am the LORD, when I open your graves, and raise you from your graves, O my people. And I will put my Spirit within you, and you shall live, and I will place you in your own land. Then you shall know that I am the LORD; I have spoken, and I will do it, declares the LORD." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Ezekiel sees a valley of dry bones, a picture of Israel in exile, utterly hopeless. God commands him to prophesy, and the bones come together, flesh covers them and breath enters them. God promises to put his Spirit in his people and bring them home. Only God can bring life from death.

4.reflection:
Why did Israel's kings fail? What did this point to?

How is the promise to David fulfilled in Jesus?

Read Jeremiah 31:31-34. What is new about the new covenant?

How does Ezekiel 37 give hope to those who feel spiritually dead?

5.title: The Promise Kept in Christ
5.overview:
The time is fulfilled. After centuries of waiting, Jesus came preaching: The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand; repent and believe in the gospel (Mark 1:15). Everything the Old Testament promised was arriving in him.

All the promises. For all the promises of God find their Yes in him (2 Cor 1:20). Jesus is the offspring of the woman who crushes the serpent. He is the offspring of Abraham in whom the nations are blessed. He is the prophet like Moses, the Passover lamb and the true temple. He is the Son of David, the King who reigns forever. He is the suffering servant who bears our sins, and the one who pours out the Spirit.

The true Israel. Jesus relives Israel's story and succeeds where Israel failed. Like Israel, he came out of Egypt (Matt 2:15). Like Israel, he passed through water and was tested in the wilderness, but he did not fall (Matt 4:1-11). Where Israel was an unfaithful vine, Jesus is the true vine (John 15:1).

The cross and resurrection. At the cross, the serpent bruised his heel; Jesus died. But by his death he defeated the devil and paid for sin. On the third day he rose. The new creation began in a garden tomb.

Reading the Old Testament. After his resurrection, Jesus told his disciples, everything written about me in the Law of Moses and the Prophets and the Psalms must be fulfilled (Luke 24:44). The whole Old Testament points to him, through promises, patterns, people and institutions. To read it rightly is to see Christ.
5.theology:
Christ-centred, not allegorical: Seeing Christ in the Old Testament does not mean finding hidden meanings in every detail. It means following the storyline, the promises and the patterns that God himself built into history, as the New Testament writers did.

Already and not yet: In Christ the kingdom has come, but it has not yet come in its fullness. We live between his first and second comings. The Kingdom of God study explores this further.

Continuity and discontinuity: The one story of salvation runs through both Testaments. Yet with Christ, much changes: the ceremonial law is fulfilled, the people of God include all nations, and the Spirit is poured out on all believers.
5.examples:
Then: The Ethiopian official was reading Isaiah 53 and asked Philip who the prophet was speaking about. Then Philip opened his mouth, and beginning with this Scripture he told him the good news about Jesus (Acts 8:35). The Old Testament led him straight to Christ.

Now: A man who grew up hearing Bible stories as moral lessons ("Be brave like David") hears a sermon that shows how David's victory over Goliath points to Christ's victory for his people. He realises the Bible is not mainly about him being a hero, but about Christ the true champion.

A simple test: When you read an Old Testament story, do you ask "How does this point to Christ?"

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "O foolish ones, and slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken! Was it not necessary that the Christ should suffer these things and enter into his glory?" And beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, he interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Two disciples on the road to Emmaus were confused and disappointed. The risen Jesus rebuked them for being slow to believe the prophets. Then, beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, he showed them the things about himself in all the Scriptures. The Old Testament is a book about Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he said to them, "These are my words that I spoke to you while I was still with you, that everything written about me in the Law of Moses and the Prophets and the Psalms must be fulfilled." Then he opened their minds to understand the Scriptures, and said to them, "Thus it is written, that the Christ should suffer and on the third day rise from the dead, and that repentance for the forgiveness of sins should be proclaimed in his name to all nations, beginning from Jerusalem. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Jesus opened his disciples' minds to understand the Scriptures. Everything in the Law, the Prophets and the Psalms about him had to be fulfilled. The Christ would suffer and rise, and repentance and forgiveness would be proclaimed to all nations. The whole story leads to the cross, the resurrection and the mission.

verseByVerse.quote: As surely as God is faithful, our word to you has not been Yes and No. For the Son of God, Jesus Christ, whom we proclaimed among you, Silvanus and Timothy and I, was not Yes and No, but in him it is always Yes. For all the promises of God find their Yes in him. That is why it is through him that we utter our Amen to God for his glory. And it is God who establishes us with you in Christ, and has anointed us, and who has also put his seal on us and given us his Spirit in our hearts as a guarantee. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul defends his reliability by pointing to God's faithfulness. All the promises of God find their Yes in Christ. Through him we say our Amen. God has anointed and sealed us and given us his Spirit as a guarantee. Every promise is secure in Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: Now after John was arrested, Jesus came into Galilee, proclaiming the gospel of God, and saying, "The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand; repent and believe in the gospel." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Jesus begins his ministry with a summary of his message. The time is fulfilled: the waiting is over. The kingdom of God is at hand: God's reign is arriving in Jesus. The response: repent and believe. This is the hinge of the whole biblical story.

5.reflection:
Name five Old Testament promises or patterns fulfilled in Christ.

How did Jesus relive and fulfil Israel's story?

What does it mean that all God's promises find their Yes in Christ?

How can you read the Old Testament with Christ at the centre without forcing meanings onto it?

6.title: To the Nations and the New Creation
6.overview:
The Spirit poured out. After his resurrection and ascension, Jesus poured out the Holy Spirit at Pentecost. The scattering of Babel began to be reversed: people from many nations heard the gospel in their own languages (Acts 2:5-11).

To the ends of the earth. Jesus sent his disciples to be his witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth (Acts 1:8). The book of Acts follows this map. The gospel spread from Jews to Samaritans to Gentiles, from Jerusalem to Rome. The promise to Abraham that all nations would be blessed was being fulfilled.

One new people. In Christ, Jews and Gentiles are united in one body. Paul calls this a mystery now revealed: This mystery is that the Gentiles are fellow heirs, members of the same body, and partakers of the promise in Christ Jesus through the gospel (Eph 3:6). The church is the people of God, made up of every nation.

The story continues. The church lives in the final chapter before the ending. We proclaim the gospel, make disciples, suffer and wait. Christ reigns now, and his kingdom grows through the gospel.

The ending. The story ends with Christ's return, the resurrection of the dead, the final judgment and the new creation. John sees a great multitude that no one could number, from every nation, from all tribes and peoples and languages, standing before the throne and before the Lamb (Rev 7:9). Then he sees the new heaven and new earth, and the holy city coming down. Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man (Rev 21:3).

Eden restored and surpassed. In the new creation, God's people are in God's place, under God's rule, enjoying his blessing forever. The tree of life is there, the curse is gone, and God's servants see his face (Rev 22:1-5). The story that began in a garden ends in a garden city, far more glorious than Eden.
6.theology:
The church and Israel: The church does not replace Israel as if God changed his plans. Believing Gentiles are grafted into the one olive tree of God's people (Rom 11:17-24). The church is the fulfilment of God's promise to bless all nations through Abraham.

The amillennial reading: Christ reigns now from heaven, and at his one return there will be a general resurrection, the final judgment and the eternal state. The End Times Models study explains the alternatives.

Our place in the story: Every Christian has a part in this story. We are not spectators but participants, living between the resurrection and the return of Christ, called to bear witness until he comes.
6.examples:
Then: In Antioch, believers from Jewish and Gentile backgrounds worshipped together. The church there sent out Paul and Barnabas as the first missionaries to the Gentile world (Acts 13:1-3). The promise to Abraham was spreading across the nations.

Now: A church in a multicultural city has members from twenty nations. During communion, a visitor looks around and is moved: this is a small picture of Revelation 7:9. The story God began with Abraham is being fulfilled before his eyes.

A simple test: Where do you fit in the big story of the Bible? What is your part in it?

verseByVerse.quote: So when they had come together, they asked him, "Lord, will you at this time restore the kingdom to Israel?" He said to them, "It is not for you to know times or seasons that the Father has fixed by his own authority. But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you, and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth." And when he had said these things, as they were looking on, he was lifted up, and a cloud took him out of their sight. And while they were gazing into heaven as he went, behold, two men stood by them in white robes, and said, "Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into heaven? This Jesus, who was taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way as you saw him go into heaven." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The disciples ask whether Jesus will now restore the kingdom to Israel. Jesus tells them the timing is the Father's business. Their task is to be witnesses to the ends of the earth, empowered by the Spirit. Then he ascends, and angels promise his return. The church lives between the ascension and the return.

verseByVerse.quote: When you read this, you can perceive my insight into the mystery of Christ, which was not made known to the sons of men in other generations as it has now been revealed to his holy apostles and prophets by the Spirit. This mystery is that the Gentiles are fellow heirs, members of the same body, and partakers of the promise in Christ Jesus through the gospel. Of this gospel I was made a minister according to the gift of God's grace, which was given me by the working of his power. To me, though I am the very least of all the saints, this grace was given, to preach to the Gentiles the unsearchable riches of Christ, and to bring to light for everyone what is the plan of the mystery hidden for ages in God, who created all things, so that through the church the manifold wisdom of God might now be made known to the rulers and authorities in the heavenly places. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul explains the mystery hidden for ages: that Gentiles are fellow heirs with Israel in Christ. Through the church, God's manifold wisdom is now made known even to the heavenly powers. The church of Jews and Gentiles is a display of God's wisdom to the universe.

verseByVerse.quote: After this I looked, and behold, a great multitude that no one could number, from every nation, from all tribes and peoples and languages, standing before the throne and before the Lamb, clothed in white robes, with palm branches in their hands, and crying out with a loud voice, "Salvation belongs to our God who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb!" And all the angels were standing around the throne and around the elders and the four living creatures, and they fell on their faces before the throne and worshiped God, saying, "Amen! Blessing and glory and wisdom and thanksgiving and honor and power and might be to our God forever and ever! Amen." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: John sees a countless multitude from every nation, tribe, people and language, standing before the throne and the Lamb. They cry out that salvation belongs to God and the Lamb. The promise to Abraham is fulfilled: all the families of the earth are blessed.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I saw a new heaven and a new earth, for the first heaven and the first earth had passed away, and the sea was no more. And I saw the holy city, new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband. And I heard a loud voice from the throne saying, "Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man. He will dwell with them, and they will be his people, and God himself will be with them as their God. He will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more, neither shall there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain anymore, for the former things have passed away." And he who was seated on the throne said, "Behold, I am making all things new." Also he said, "Write this down, for these words are trustworthy and true." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The new heaven and new earth arrive, and the holy city comes down from God. God dwells with his people, wipes every tear and abolishes death. He makes all things new. The whole story of Scripture reaches its goal: God with his people forever in a renewed creation.

6.reflection:
How does Pentecost reverse Babel?

Read Ephesians 3:4-10. Why is the church of Jews and Gentiles so important?

How does Revelation 7:9 fulfil the promise to Abraham?

What is your part in the big story of the Bible right now?
